problem: Reactive RL navigation policies for legged robots choose actions from current observations and short memory, so they respond late to moving obstacles. World-model methods add anticipation but keep reconstruction/imagination active at inference, which is costly on onboard hardware.
motivation: Collision risk in dynamic scenes depends on short-horizon obstacle motion, not just current positions. The paper asks whether predictive supervision used only in training, with the predictor discarded at deployment, can shape the recurrent state to encode anticipatory dynamics at zero inference cost.
key_idea: Add a training-only JEPA-style one-step latent predictor on the LSTM-SRU hidden state, with SIGReg variance/decorrelation regularization against collapse, and discard it at inference.
insight: The gain comes from the predictive gradient shaping the recurrent state, and only when regularized: removing SIGReg drops Nav SR to 86.0% (CR 12.1%), worse than the no-WM baseline at 90.7%, while with SIGReg SR rises to 94.4%. On DynObs, collisions fall from 14.0% to 3.8%, suggesting the hidden state encodes short-horizon obstacle motion. An MLP predictor (0.4M params) nearly matches a Transformer (2.1M, 95.3% SR).
method: Reactive backbone: depth (64x40, conv/VAE features), 16-d proprioception/goal and up to 12 obstacles x 11 features are fused via robot-conditioned cross-attention (proprioception as query) and fed to an LSTM-SRU with odometry-based spatial modulation; actor/critic read h_t (512-d).
Predictive branch: an MLP predictor g_theta(h_t, a_t) predicts h_{t+1}; loss is MSE/d against stop-gradient target, with LayerNorm on h_t and z_t detached from the predictor; training-only.
SIGReg: penalty on per-dimension batch std deviation from 1 plus squared off-diagonal batch correlations of h_t (VICReg-like) to prevent collapse; alpha_pred=0.03, alpha_sigreg=0.003.

RL training: MDPO with asymmetric actor-critic (critic gets privileged obstacle/terrain states), Muon+AdamW, shaped reward (goal kernels, -50 failure penalty, smoothness terms), dynamic obstacle speed curriculum, domain randomization, stereo depth noise.
Hierarchical control: the policy outputs SE(2) velocity commands at 5 Hz, passed through tanh, scaling and low-pass filtering to a frozen Go2 locomotion controller at 50 Hz.
Inference: predictor and SIGReg are dropped; the deployed controller is the reactive backbone only, run on a Jetson Orin.

setting.backbone: LSTM-SRU recurrent policy with cross-attention obstacle encoder and depth CNN/VAE encoder, trained with MDPO from scratch; frozen pretrained Go2 locomotion controller below it
setting.model_size: predictor 0.4M (MLP) for training only; total policy size not given
setting.training_data: RL in Isaac Sim 4.5 / Isaac Lab 2.1.1, 20,000 iterations x 4,096 parallel envs, ~3 days on 4x RTX 4090D; maze, pillar, stairs and dynamic-obstacle terrains; no external data
setting.observation: 64x40 depth image + proprioception/goal features + explicit obstacle features (GT physics with noise in sim; depth-YOLO detection/tracking on real robot)
setting.action_space: continuous high-level velocity command (vx, vy, omega) at 5 Hz, executed by a frozen low-level locomotion policy
setting.privileged: Critic only, at training, uses true obstacle states and terrain; in simulation the actor's obstacle features come from ground-truth physics state with noise; none at real-robot test time beyond detected obstacles

numbers.eval_set_note: 107 episodes across 8 parallel envs on the paper's own Isaac Lab terrains
numbers.extra: success radius 2 m; own simulator, not a standard benchmark

numbers.eval_set_note: 107 episodes across 8 parallel envs; moving obstacles at 0.3-0.8 m/s (WANDER, CROSS, ARC)

numbers_note: Benchmarks are custom Isaac Lab tasks, not standard ones; splits are labelled 'test' as a placeholder. No standard navigation benchmark (SR/SPL/NE on R2R etc.) is used.
results: SRU-WM reaches 94.4% SR on Nav and 96.2% SR / 3.8% CR on DynObs. It beats NavRL (41.5% / 52.3% SR) and NavDP (11.2% / 19.2% SR), and improves on its own reactive SRU baseline (90.7% / 86.0% SR, 14.0% CR on DynObs). Zero-shot deployment on a Unitree Go2 is shown qualitatively indoors and outdoors.
limitations: Only one-step prediction; multi-step rollout is not evaluated, and longer-horizon dynamics are untested.

Small evaluation (107 episodes), no seeds or variance reported. Baselines are adapted to a different sensor/action setup (NavDP inference latency causes many timeouts), so the comparison is not controlled. The real-robot evidence is qualitative only, with no quantitative success rates.
Relies on explicit obstacle features (GT in sim, YOLO tracking on the real robot), and the Nav ablation gains are modest (+3.7 SR).
